questions.q: Meena wants a scrapbook of leaves and flowers from the nature walk. The activity asks students not to disturb plants. Which plan follows the instructions?
questions.a: Collect only leaves and flowers already fallen on the path. The activity allows collecting fallen leaves or flowers and says not to pluck leaves and flowers.
o: Collect only leaves and flowers already fallen on the path
Pluck one leaf from every plant she passes so that the set is complete
Take one flower from each plant, since a single flower will not matter
Break small twigs so that the leaves can be pressed in the scrapbook

questions.q: Priya says the nature walk records of two students are both correct even though one student listed 9 plants and the other listed 12. Give one reason, from the chapter's activities, why the lists may differ, and say what this suggests about the variety in the park.
questions.a: Different students notice different plants and the park holds many kinds, so no single list shows all of them; it suggests that the park has more variety than any one list records.
s: Reason: students observe and record different plants, so the lists differ
Inference: the park has a variety larger than what one list shows

questions.q:
Statement 1: The variety of plants and animals found in a region contributes to the biodiversity of that region.
Statement 2: Biodiversity of a region includes only its animals, since plants have no role to play in it.
Statement 3: Animals help in spreading seeds after eating fruits, so plants and animals in a region depend on each other.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 only. Statement 2 is false: trees, grasses and other plants are part of biodiversity and give food and shelter to animals.
o: Statements 1 and 3 only
Statement 2 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
All three statements

questions.q:
Villagers near a forest edge surveyed three patches of land. Patch A: 14 kinds of plants and 11 kinds of animals. Patch B: about 500 bushes, all of 6 kinds, and 4 kinds of animals. Patch C: 19 kinds of plants and 5 kinds of animals; it holds the only old fruit trees in the area, and hornbills and mynas that roost in patch A fly there every day to eat the fruit. The panchayat can fence and protect only one patch this year.
(a) Which patch has the greatest biodiversity, and why is patch B not the answer even though it has the most plants?
(b) Name the two ways, given in the chapter, in which the birds of patch A and the fruit trees of patch C help each other.
(c) If patch C is cleared, what may happen to the birds of patch A, and to the number of young fruit trees in the area over the years?
(d) Decide whether to protect patch A or patch C. Justify your choice using (a) to (c) and say what is risked by not protecting the other.
questions.a: (a) Patch A, with 25 kinds (C has 24, B has 10). Biodiversity is the variety of kinds, so B's 500 bushes of only 6 kinds add little variety. (b) The trees give the birds food (and shelter); the birds spread the trees' seeds after eating the fruit. (c) The birds lose their food and may leave patch A; fewer seeds are spread, so fewer young fruit trees come up. (d) Either choice is acceptable when justified. Protect A: it holds the most kinds now, but the birds may still lose their food in C. Protect C: it feeds the birds of A and keeps the fruit trees growing, though A's 11 animal kinds stay exposed.
s: Patch A with 25 kinds, and B rejected because biodiversity counts kinds, not the number of plants
Two-way link: trees give food to birds, birds spread the trees' seeds
Effect of clearing C on the birds of A and on young fruit trees
A choice between A and C that uses the earlier parts and names the risk to the patch left out

questions.q:
A forest guard fenced a plot so that fruit-eating birds could not enter it. After one year, 2 ber seedlings had come up inside the fence and 18 in an open plot of the same size next to it, where the same ber trees grew.
(a) Give the chapter's explanation for the difference.
(b) What does this suggest would happen to the ber trees of the region over many years if the fruit-eating birds left?
questions.a: (a) Animals help in spreading seeds after eating fruits; the birds carried and dropped ber seeds in the open plot but could not reach the fenced one. (b) Fewer new ber plants would come up, so the number of ber trees would fall over the years: the plants depend on the animals too.
s: Part (a): birds spread the seeds after eating the fruits, and could not do so inside the fence
Part (b): fewer young ber trees over the years, showing the plants depend on animals

questions.q: Here is a conclusion: 'If the fruit-eating animals leave a forest, fewer new trees of some kinds may grow there.' Write a short real-life situation (two or three sentences) that supports this conclusion, naming the tree, the animal and the step that goes missing.
questions.a: For example: monkeys and bulbuls eat jamun fruits in a village grove and drop the seeds far from the parent tree, where new jamun saplings come up. When a highway scares the animals away, the seeds stay under the parent trees and few new jamun trees grow.
s: A tree and a fruit-eating animal named in a realistic setting
The missing step: the animal no longer spreads the seeds after eating the fruit
Link to the conclusion: fewer new trees because plants and animals depend on each other

questions.q:
Three friends merge their nature-walk lists into one class register for their park. Ananya listed 10 kinds of plants and animals, Bilal 8 and Charu 7. Four kinds appear on exactly two of the lists and one kind appears on all three; every other kind appears on one list only. Charu also heard three bird calls that she could not match to any bird the group saw. Their teacher says that more than 100 kinds of plants and animals have been seen in this park over the years.
(i) How many different kinds are in the register?
(ii) What percentage of the register's kinds did Ananya's list hold (one decimal place)?
(iii) Should the three unmatched calls be counted as new kinds of birds? Give a reason from the chapter.
(iv) Bilal says: 'Our register is the biodiversity of the park.' Use the numbers and the teacher's remark to judge his claim.
(v) Suggest two changes to the next walk that would make the register fuller, each with a reason taken from the chapter's activities.
questions.a: (i) The lists add to 25 = (kinds on one list) + 2 x 4 + 3 x 1, so 14 kinds are on one list only and the register holds 14 + 4 + 1 = 19 kinds. (ii) 10/19 x 100 = 52.6%. (iii) They may be counted only if they are three different calls not made by any bird already listed, because each bird has its own unique chirp; otherwise the group should check them first. (iv) Not right: 19 kinds is far fewer than the 100-plus kinds known from the park, and Ananya alone saw only about half of the register; the register is a record of what they observed, while the park's biodiversity is the whole variety found there. (v) For example: walk at another time and note the weather, since conditions change what is seen; listen carefully to bird calls; look at insects as well as larger animals; add plants and animals seen on the way to school.
s: Register size: 14 + 4 + 1 = 19 kinds
Ananya's share: 10/19 x 100 = 52.6%
Unmatched calls judged using each bird's unique chirp
Claim judged with 19 against more than 100: a register records only what was observed
Two improvements, each tied to an instruction of the chapter's activities

questions.q:
A plant table records: grass, stem soft and thin, a single leaf growing alternately from different points; tulsi, stem hard and thin, a pair of leaves in opposite directions; neem, stem hard and thick. Rohan says: 'In its stem, tulsi sits halfway between grass and neem.'
(a) Use both stem features to test his statement.
(b) Name the leaf feature that separates tulsi from grass, and how it differs.
questions.a: (a) He is right in a sense: tulsi is thin like grass but hard like neem, so it shares one stem feature with each. (b) Leaf arrangement: tulsi has a pair of leaves in opposite directions, while grass has single leaves growing alternately.
s: Part (a): thin like grass, hard like neem, so one shared feature with each
Part (b): leaf arrangement, paired and opposite against single and alternate

questions.q: Four students each write one note while observing the same plant on a nature walk. Only one note belongs under the 'Leaves (shape/arrangement)' heading of the plant table. Which note is it?
questions.a: Leaves grow in pairs facing opposite ways. Arrangement of leaves is a leaf feature; stem hardness and height describe the stem and the colour and scent describe the flowers.
o: Leaves grow in pairs facing opposite ways
The stem is hard and thin when bent gently
The petals are pinkish purple and have a sweet scent
The plant is about as tall as a Class 6 student

questions.q: True or False? Because each member of a region's biodiversity has its own role, plants can be removed from a park without any effect on the animals living there. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. Trees provide food and shelter to some birds and other animals, so removing plants affects the animals that depend on them.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: plants give animals food and shelter, so animals are affected

questions.q: In Table 2.2, a student notes for the ant 'Have six legs' and for the crow 'Carrying a twig in its beak'. A classmate says these notes should be dropped because the table has only the columns for habitat, food and movement. What is the best reply?
questions.a: The notes belong, since the table has a column for any other features. Table 2.2 keeps a last column for any other observations and features, where such notes are written.
o: The notes belong, since the table has a column for any other features
The notes are wrong because only habitat, food and movement may be written
The notes are correct only if the animal is also drawn in the notebook
The notes are wrong because six legs is a plant feature and not an animal feature

questions.q: Park P has 200 plants of only 3 kinds and 2 kinds of animals. Park Q has 60 plants of 15 kinds and 12 kinds of animals. Using the meaning of biodiversity in this chapter, which statement is correct?
questions.a: Park Q, because it has more kinds of plants and animals. Biodiversity is the variety of plants and animals in a region, not how many individuals there are.
o: Park Q, because it has more kinds of plants and animals
Park P has the greater biodiversity because it has the larger number of plants
Both parks have equal biodiversity because both are parks in the same region
Park P has the greater biodiversity because three kinds of plants give a stronger shelter

questions.q:
Two students walk through the same park on the same day. Asha walks at 7 a.m., just after rain, and records 14 kinds of animals. Kabir walks at 1 p.m. in the heat and records 5 kinds.
(a) Which instruction of the nature-walk activity would help the class explain the difference later?
(b) Kabir concludes that the park lost biodiversity between morning and afternoon. Is he right? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) The instruction to note the weather conditions (hot, cold, windy and so on) along with the observations. (b) No. Biodiversity is the variety of plants and animals found in the region, and it did not change in six hours; each list shows only what that student saw at that time, so the two lists should be combined.
s: Part (a): noting the weather conditions with each record
Part (b): No, a single walk records what was seen, not the region's whole variety

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Dr Raghu described the different chirps of the different birds in the park as an example of diversity.
Reason (R): Maniram chacha could mimic the calls of several different birds.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. Both statements are in the chapter, but A rests on each bird having its own unique chirp, not on a person being able to copy the calls.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: On a walk, Lata finds two plants that both have hard stems and pinkish-purple flowers. She writes: 'These are the same kind of plant.' Which further observation would best test her conclusion?
questions.a: Compare their leaf shape and arrangement, and their height. Plants vary in many features (height, stem, leaf shape and arrangement, flowers), so matching two features is not enough; flower colour checked again or a flower count does not test the other features.
o: Compare their leaf shape and arrangement, and their height
Smell the flowers once more, since scent decides the plant
Check the colour of the flowers again in brighter light
Count the flowers, since the same kind has the same number

questions.q:
An animal table has the columns: place where it lives, food it eats, the way it moves, and any other observations and features. For a squirrel, Neha writes four notes: 'eats nuts', 'lives in a hole in a tree trunk', 'runs and climbs', 'has a bushy tail'.
(a) Which note belongs in the last column, and why not under the way it moves?
(b) Both the crow and the squirrel live on trees. Which column of the table shows that they still differ, and how?
questions.a: (a) 'Has a bushy tail': it is a feature of the body, not a place, a food or a way of moving. (b) The way they move: the crow flies and walks, while the squirrel runs and climbs (food also differs: insects against nuts).
s: Part (a): the bushy tail, a body feature, goes in the other-observations column
Part (b): the movement (or food) column shows the difference

questions.q: Mohan says: 'For my scrapbook I need leaves and flowers, so I will pluck them from the plants on the walk.' Is he right? Give your answer with a reason and a better plan.
questions.a: Partly right. He needs leaves and flowers, which the activity allows him to collect, but plucking is not allowed; he should collect fallen leaves or flowers.
s: Verdict: partly right, since collecting for a scrapbook is allowed
Fault: the activity says do not pluck leaves and flowers
Better plan: collect fallen leaves or flowers

questions.q: Imran claims: 'A park with 300 crows has more biodiversity than a park with 4 crows, 3 monkeys, 6 kinds of butterflies and 20 kinds of plants, because it has more animals.' Check his claim.
questions.a: No. Biodiversity is the variety of plants and animals in a region, not the number of animals. The second park has more variety.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Reason: biodiversity is variety of kinds of plants and animals, not a head count
Comparison: the second park has many kinds of plants and animals, so it has the greater variety

questions.q:
The gardener of a colony park proposes to remove all trees and bushes and keep only a mown lawn, because the park will then be easier to clean. A group of Class 6 students argues against it.
(i) State what the birds of the park lose if the trees go.
(ii) State what the trees would no longer receive if the birds and other fruit-eating animals leave.
(iii) Say what happens to the variety of plants and animals in the park.
(iv) Give one genuine advantage of the gardener's plan.
(v) Recommend a plan that you think is fair to both sides and justify it.
questions.a: (i) Food and shelter. (ii) The help of animals in spreading seeds after eating fruits. (iii) It falls, so the park's biodiversity is reduced. (iv) Less cleaning and easier upkeep. (v) Keep the trees and bushes and clear a lawn area or fallen leaves regularly; this keeps variety and a clean park.
s: Birds lose the food and shelter that trees provide
Trees lose the seed-spreading help of animals
Variety of plants and animals falls, so biodiversity falls
A real advantage of the plan such as easier cleaning
A balanced recommendation that keeps trees and justifies the choice

questions.q:
A Class 6 in Nashik walked twice through their school garden and noted what they saw. First walk: 9 kinds of plants and 6 kinds of animals. Second walk: 8 kinds of plants and 5 kinds of animals. Two kinds of plants and one kind of animal were seen on both walks. Of the animal kinds in their register, 4 live on trees, 3 nest in soil, 2 live in water and 1 lives on land as well as in water. The school wants to cut three tall trees to make a play area; these trees are the places where four of the tree-living animal kinds live.
(a) How many different kinds of plants and of animals did the class record altogether?
(b) What percentage of the animal kinds live in water at least part of the time?
(c) Which idea of the chapter explains why the cutting would matter to the four animal kinds?
(d) The school can instead use a bare patch behind the building, but it floods every monsoon and can then be used for only about 7 of the 10 school months, while the trees site can be used all year. Choose one site and justify it using your answers.
questions.a: (a) 15 kinds of plants and 10 kinds of animals. (b) 30%. (c) Trees provide food and shelter to birds and other animals, so these animals depend on them. (d) Either site is acceptable when the cost is named. Bare patch: the four tree-living kinds (40% of the animal kinds) keep their homes and food, at the cost of about three months without play each year. Trees site: play all year, at the cost of the homes of four animal kinds and the garden's variety.
s: Union of the two walks: 9 + 8 - 2 = 15 plants and 6 + 5 - 1 = 10 animals
Animals in water at least partly: (2 + 1)/10 x 100 = 30%
Dependence: trees provide food and shelter to animals
A site choice that weighs the lost animal homes against the months of play lost to flooding

questions.q: In Activity 2.2, Class 6A drew 23 different plants and animals on the blackboard and Class 6B drew 19. Eight of these were drawn by both classes. Together the two classes drew ___ different kinds of plants and animals.

For Science Day, Class 6 of a school in Coimbatore must label 8 potted plants. Their notes: P1 short, green, soft stem, has flowers. P2 tall, brown, hard, thick stem, branches start high up, no flowers seen. P3 medium height, several brown, hard, thin stems branching at the soil, has flowers. P4 weak stem winding up a stick, has flowers. P5 short, green, soft stem, no flowers. P6 weak stem spreading over the soil, has flowers. P7 like P3 but no flowers. P8 short, green, soft stem, has flowers. The display may group the pots by stem features or by presence of flowers. The labels must be printed this evening: the stem grouping needs five label boards, the flower grouping two.
(a) Place each pot in a group by its stem features.
(b) Group the pots by presence of flowers and give the size of each bundle.
(c) Which grouping gives more even bundles? Compare the largest bundle of each as a percentage of 8.
(d) Choose a grouping for the display, justify it with your answers and state what the other grouping would have shown.
questions.a: (a) Herbs P1, P5, P8; tree P2; shrubs P3, P7; climber P4; creeper P6. (b) With flowers: P1, P3, P4, P6, P8 (5); without: P2, P5, P7 (3). (c) The stem grouping: its largest bundle is 3 of 8 (37.5%), against 5 of 8 (62.5%) for flowers. (d) Either is acceptable when justified. Stem grouping: shows five kinds of plant body and more even bundles, but needs five boards by tonight. Flower grouping: quicker with two boards, but tells visitors only whether a plant has flowers.
s: Stem groups: herbs P1 P5 P8, tree P2, shrubs P3 P7, climber P4, creeper P6
Flower bundles: 5 with flowers and 3 without
Largest bundle 3/8 = 37.5% for stems against 5/8 = 62.5% for flowers
A justified choice that weighs boards and time against what the display shows

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A plant with a weak stem that lies along the ground is called a creeper.
Reason (R): Creepers need a support such as a stick or wall to climb and grow.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false. Needing a support such as a stick or wall to climb describes climbers; creepers creep along the ground.
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
In Gita's garden, a money plant with a weak stem grows up a pole it is tied to, and a pumpkin plant with a weak stem spreads across the soil.
(a) Name the group of each plant.
(b) Both stems are weak. Which observation decided the two groups?
questions.a: (a) The money plant is a climber; the pumpkin plant is a creeper. (b) Whether the weak stem climbs up a support or creeps along the ground; weakness of the stem alone cannot separate them because both have it.
s: Part (a): money plant climber, pumpkin creeper
Part (b): climbing on a support against creeping on the ground, since both stems are weak

questions.q:
In Activity 2.4 students gently bend the stem of each plant.
(a) What does bending a stem tell them?
(b) A plant is short, its stem is green and bends very easily. Which of the three groups (herb, shrub, tree) does it most likely belong to, and why?
questions.a: (a) Whether the stem is tender or hard (stiff). (b) A herb, because herbs are typically small with soft, green stems.
s: Part (a): the hardness of the stem, soft or stiff
Part (b): herb, as a small plant with a soft green stem

questions.q: Asha observes a plant about as tall as her chest. It has several brown, hard stems that begin to branch just above the soil, and none of them is as thick as the trunk of a mango tree. How should she record its group?
questions.a: Shrub, as its hard brown stems branch close to the ground. Shrubs have many brown woody stems, hard but not as thick as a tree's, which start branching very close to the ground.
o: Shrub, as its hard brown stems branch close to the ground
Tree, because its stems are brown, hard and woody like a mango tree's
Herb, because it is shorter than a mango tree
Climber, because it has several stems growing from one place

questions.q: Write a row for a table like Table 2.3 for a plant that you would call a shrub: give its height, stem colour, hardness, thickness and where its branches appear. Say which one feature separates it from a tree.
questions.a: For example: medium height, brown, hard, thin, branches close to the ground. It differs from a tree in that its stem is thinner and branches start low.
s: A complete row of height, colour, hardness, thickness and branching
Values consistent with a shrub
One separating feature from a tree

questions.q: Show that one plant cannot be both a tree and a herb at the same time, using features of the stem.
questions.a: A tree has a hard, thick, brown woody stem, but a herb has a soft, green stem; a stem cannot be hard and soft or brown and green at once.
s: Tree stem: hard, thick, brown and woody
Herb stem: soft and green
The features contradict, so no single plant fits both

questions.q:
Statement 1: Herbs typically have hard, thick, brown woody stems with branches high up on the stem.
Statement 2: Shrubs often have many brown woody stems that begin branching very close to the ground and are not as thick as a tree's.
Statement 3: Climbers have weak stems and need support to climb and grow.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 only. Statement 1 describes a tree, not a herb; herbs are small with soft, green stems.
o: Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 1 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only

questions.q: Tara says: 'Rose and mango both have brown hard stems with branches, so both are trees.' Is she right? Use the chapter's description of each group.
questions.a: No. The mango is tall with a thick stem and branches starting high; the rose is medium in height with a thinner stem branching close to the ground, so it is a shrub.
s: Verdict: she is wrong because brown and hard fit both trees and shrubs
Mango fits a tree: tall, thick, branches higher up
Rose fits a shrub: medium height, thin, branches close to the ground

questions.q: Tanvi copies a plant-grouping table with six columns: height, stem colour, tender or hard, thick or thin, where the branches start, and flower scent. Her teacher says one column will not help her name a plant as a tree, a shrub or a herb. Which column is it?
questions.a: Flower scent. Height, stem colour, hardness, thickness and where the branches start are the features used to place a plant as a tree, shrub or herb; scent belongs to the flower record.
o: Flower scent
Where the branches start
Stem colour
Thick or thin

questions.q:
Aman groups eight plants into short, medium and tall. Rina groups the same eight into those with flowers and those without.
(a) Why can the two groupings be different even though both are correct?
(b) State one benefit that both groupings give.
questions.a: (a) They used different common features as the basis. (b) Grouping makes it easier to understand and study plants through their similarities and differences.
s: Part (a): different features were chosen as the basis of grouping
Part (b): easier study and understanding through similarities and differences

questions.q:
A school nursery logs seven plants.
P1: tall, brown, hard, thick, branches high up.
P2: medium, brown, hard, thin, branches near the ground.
P3: short, green, tender, thin.
P4: tall, brown, hard, thick, branches high up.
P5: short, green, tender, thin.
P6: medium, brown, hard, thin, branches near the ground.
P7: short, green, tender, thin.
(i) Name the group of each plant.
(ii) Name the two stem features that, on their own, separate the herbs from all the other plants.
(iii) The herbs share one stem feature with the shrubs. Name it and explain why it cannot be used alone to group these plants.
(iv) The herb records have no entry for where the branches start. Explain why the nursery could still place them.
(v) The nursery also wants to group the plants by presence of flowers. Why is this a different basis, and why can it give different bundles?
questions.a: (i) P1 and P4 trees; P2 and P6 shrubs; P3, P5 and P7 herbs. (ii) Stem colour (green against brown) and stem hardness (tender against hard). (iii) Thinness: herbs and shrubs both have thin stems, so a thin-stem bundle would mix P2 and P6 with the herbs. (iv) A short plant with a soft green stem already fits the herb description, so the branching entry is not needed to place it. (v) Flowers are a different common feature from the stem; groups made on different features need not match.
s: Groups: trees P1 P4, shrubs P2 P6, herbs P3 P5 P7
Colour and hardness each separate the herbs
Thin stem is shared by herbs and shrubs, so it would mix them
Short, soft, green stem is enough to place a herb
Presence of flowers is another common feature, so it can give different bundles

questions.q: Ten plants in a nursery have hard brown woody stems. Four of them are thick-stemmed, taller than all the other six, with branches starting high up; six are thinner with branches starting close to the ground. Farida says the four are trees and the six are shrubs. Check her claim.
questions.a: Yes. Tall plants with hard, thick brown stems and branches high up are trees; shorter plants with hard, thinner brown stems branching near the ground are shrubs.
s: Verdict: she is right
Four plants match the tree description: taller, thick stem, high branching
Six plants match the shrub description of thinner stems branching near the ground

questions.q:
A table records mango as tall, brown, hard, thick; rose as medium height, brown, hard, thin; tomato as short, green, tender, thin.
(a) Which two stem features separate the tomato from both the mango and the rose?
(b) Which stem feature separates the mango from the rose, though both are brown and hard?
questions.a: (a) The tomato's stem is green and tender (soft). (b) Thickness: the mango's stem is thick and the rose's is thin.
s: Part (a): green colour and tender nature of the tomato stem
Part (b): thick for mango against thin for rose

questions.q: Plant P has a weak stem and rises up a bamboo stick tied beside it. Plant Q has a weak stem and spreads flat along the ground. Which pair of names is correct?
questions.a: P is a climber and Q is a creeper. A plant with a weak stem that needs support to climb is a climber; one that creeps along the ground is a creeper.
o: P is a climber and Q is a creeper
P is a creeper and Q is a climber
Both are climbers because both stems are weak
P is a shrub and Q is a herb because both are small

questions.q: A group of students sorts plants only by the question 'Is the stem brown?'. Which two of the chapter's plant groups would end up together in the 'yes' bundle?
questions.a: Trees and shrubs, because both have brown woody stems. Trees and shrubs both have brown, hard, woody stems; herbs have soft green stems, so stem colour alone cannot separate a tree from a shrub.
o: Trees and shrubs, because both have brown woody stems
Herbs and shrubs, because both are small plants
Herbs and trees, because both can stand without support
Climbers and creepers, because both have brown stems

questions.q:
Rahul sorts the plants on his terrace using the questions of Activity 2.4: is it taller or shorter than me, is the stem brown or green, is it stiff or bendable, and do the branches begin near the ground or higher up? His notes: Plant A is short, green, bendable. Plant B is taller than him, brown, stiff and thick with branches starting high. Plant C is about 4 m tall, as tall as the young mango tree in the next garden and more than twice Rahul's height, brown and stiff but thin, and its branches begin near the ground.
(a) Name the group of plant A and plant B.
(b) List the features of plant C that point to a shrub and the one feature that points to a tree.
(c) State what further observation Rahul could make to be more sure about plant C.
(d) Decide what Rahul should write on plant C's label and give your reason.
questions.a: (a) Plant A is a herb and plant B is a tree. (b) Shrub features: thin stem and branches near the ground; tree feature: its great height, close to a young tree's. (c) He can compare how thick the stem is with plant B and see exactly where the branches start. (d) Shrub, as two features point to it against one for a tree, with a note that plant C is tall; a tree label is defensible only if the thickness is found to be like plant B.
s: Plant A herb (short, soft, green) and plant B tree (tall, thick, branches high)
Shrub features: thin stem and low branching; tree feature: great height
A further check such as comparing stem thickness or the height of the first branch
A justified label that weighs two shrub features against one tree feature

questions.q: True or False? Two plants can both have hard brown stems and still belong to different groups. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. A tree and a shrub both have hard brown stems, but a tree is tall with a thick stem whose branches start higher up, while a shrub has thinner stems branching near the ground.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: tree and shrub differ in thickness and in where branching starts

questions.q: Arjun (1.2 m tall) and Zoya (1.6 m tall) record the same 1.4 m plant using the Activity 2.4 question 'Is it shorter than you or taller than you?'. Arjun writes 'taller', Zoya writes 'shorter'. What does this show?
questions.a: Height judged against oneself varies by observer, so stems are used too. 1.4 m is more than 1.2 m and less than 1.6 m, so both records are honest; this is why the chapter also uses the colour, hardness and thickness of the stem and where branches start.
o: Height judged against oneself varies by observer, so stems are used too
The plant must have grown between the two observations, so both are correct
One of them made an error, since every plant group has one fixed height
Height can never be used to group plants, so the column should be removed

questions.q:
Design a short 'yes or no' key that a Class 6 student can use to place a plant as a tree, a shrub or a herb, using only features from the chapter. Then test it on mango (tall, brown, hard, thick, branches high up), rose (medium, brown, hard, thin, branches near the ground) and tomato (short, green, tender, thin).
(i) Write the first question and say which group it separates out.
(ii) Write the second question that divides the remaining plants.
(iii) Run mango through the key.
(iv) Run rose through the key.
(v) Run tomato through the key.
questions.a: (i) 'Is the stem soft and green?' Yes gives a herb. (ii) 'Is the stem thick with branches starting high up?' Yes gives a tree; No gives a shrub. (iii) Mango: stem hard, so not herb; thick with high branches, so tree. (iv) Rose: hard, thin, branching near the ground, so shrub. (v) Tomato: soft and green, so herb.
s: First question separates herbs by soft green stems
Second question separates trees from shrubs by thickness and where branches start
Mango is placed in tree
Rose is placed in shrub
Tomato is placed in herb at the first question

questions.q:
Match each description of a plant (column I) with its group (column II).
1. Tall; hard, thick, brown woody stem; branches begin high up    a. Creeper
2. Many hard brown woody stems branching near the ground, not very thick    b. Herb
3. Small plant with a soft green stem    c. Tree
4. Weak stem that moves along the ground    d. Shrub
questions.a: 1-c, 2-d, 3-b, 4-a. A tree is tall with a thick woody stem, a shrub branches near the ground, a herb is small and soft, and a creeper creeps.

questions.q: In a plant log, 18 plants have hard brown woody stems. Seven of them are tall with thick stems and branches high up; the rest have thinner stems branching close to the ground. The log holds ___ shrubs.

Ravi says: 'Chickpea seeds split into two cotyledons, so chickpea is a dicot. And because plants with reticulate venation have taproots, every reticulate-veined plant I find will surely have a taproot.' Check both parts of his claim.
questions.a: Partly right. The first part is right: a plant whose seeds have two cotyledons is a dicot, and chickpea seeds split into two parts. The second part says more than the chapter: it says plants with reticulate venation generally have taproots, so a general relation lets him predict a taproot but not be sure of it for every plant.
s: Verdict: partly right
First part correct: two cotyledons make chickpea a dicot
Second part overclaims: the venation-root relation holds generally, not surely for every plant

questions.q:
Plant 1 has reticulate venation and a taproot. Plant 2 has parallel venation and fibrous roots.
(a) Name one plant from the chapter that matches each.
(b) State whether the seed of each is a dicot or a monocot.
questions.a: (a) Plant 1: sadabahar, chickpea or hibiscus; plant 2: lemongrass, wheat or grass. (b) Plant 1 is a dicot; plant 2 is a monocot.
s: Part (a): a matching plant from the chapter for each
Part (b): dicot for plant 1 and monocot for plant 2

questions.q: On a class chart, four students each draw a plant with its leaf and its roots. The teacher circles one drawing because it shows a pairing that the chapter says is generally NOT found together. Which pairing did that drawing show?
questions.a: Parallel venation with a taproot. The chapter pairs reticulate venation with taproots and parallel venation with fibrous roots, so parallel venation with a taproot is the odd pair.
o: Parallel venation with a taproot
Reticulate venation with a taproot
Parallel venation with fibrous roots
Two cotyledons with reticulate venation

questions.q: A plant grown from a seed with one thin cotyledon will generally have parallel venation in its leaves and ___ roots.
questions.a: fibrous

questions.q: A leaf is described in a worksheet: one thick vein runs from the leaf stalk to the tip; from it, thinner veins branch out on both sides and join one another to form a net. A classmate labels the leaf 'parallel venation, like banana'. Show that this label cannot be right, and name the correct venation.
questions.a: In parallel venation the veins run parallel to one another, as in banana and grass leaves. Here thinner veins branch out on both sides of a thick middle vein and join to form a net, which is reticulate venation, as in hibiscus. A net of joining veins cannot be veins running side by side, so the label is impossible.
s: Parallel venation means veins running parallel, as in banana
The described net on both sides of a thick middle vein is reticulate venation
A joining net and side-by-side veins exclude each other, so the label is impossible

questions.q: Two seedlings are pulled out of damp soil. Seedling 1 has one main root with small side roots. Seedling 2 has a bunch of similar-sized thin roots arising from the base of the stem. Which statement matches the root systems of mustard and common grass?
questions.a: Seedling 1 has the mustard type and seedling 2 the common grass type. Mustard has a taproot, one main root with small side roots; common grass has fibrous roots, a bunch of similar thin roots.
o: Seedling 1 has the mustard type and seedling 2 the common grass type
Seedling 1 has the common grass type and seedling 2 the mustard type
Both seedlings have the mustard type because both have roots in soil
Both seedlings have the common grass type because both have thin roots

questions.q:
Ishaan digs up a seedling. From the base of its stem grow about twenty thin roots of similar size; one of them is a little longer than the rest.
(a) Name the root system and explain why the one longer root does not make it a taproot.
(b) Predict the venation of its leaves.
questions.a: (a) Fibrous roots: all the roots are thin, of similar size and arise from the base of the stem. A taproot system has one main root with small side roots arising from it, and here no root carries side roots. (b) Parallel venation.
s: Part (a): fibrous, since a taproot is one main root bearing small side roots
Part (b): parallel venation predicted

questions.q:
Manu's mother pulls a radish out of her kitchen garden and tells him the radish itself is a root. Its thick white part goes straight down, with thin small roots coming off its sides. In the next bed she has sown kidney beans, whose soaked seeds split into two parts, and wheat, whose leaves have parallel veins.
(i) What type of root system does the radish have? Give the evidence from the description.
(ii) Predict the venation of radish leaves and the number of cotyledons in a radish seed.
(iii) Predict the root system of the kidney bean plant and of the wheat plant, with a reason for each.
(iv) Manu says: 'Radish is a small plant like a herb, so it must be a monocot.' Judge his reasoning, using two small plants from the chapter's root activity.
(v) For a class display, put radish, kidney bean and wheat into two groups, one beside chickpea and one beside maize, and name the basis of the grouping.
questions.a: (i) A taproot: one main root (the radish) with small side roots arising from it. (ii) Reticulate venation and two cotyledons (a dicot). (iii) Kidney bean: two cotyledons make it a dicot, so a taproot. Wheat: parallel venation goes with fibrous roots. (iv) Wrong: being a herb is about height and stem, not about seeds. Mustard and common grass are both small plants, yet mustard has a taproot and grass has fibrous roots, so size does not tell monocot from dicot. (v) With chickpea: radish and kidney bean; with maize: wheat. The basis is the number of cotyledons (dicot and monocot).
s: Radish is a taproot: one main root with small side roots
Radish leaves reticulate, seed with two cotyledons
Kidney bean taproot (dicot); wheat fibrous (parallel venation)
Herb is a height-and-stem group; mustard and grass show small plants differ in roots
Radish and kidney bean with chickpea, wheat with maize, on cotyledon number

questions.q: True or False? In a taproot system all the roots are similar in size and arise from the base of the stem. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. That describes a fibrous root system; a taproot system has one main root with small side roots arising from it.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: a taproot system has one main root with small side roots

questions.q: Leela examines a leaf and sees a net-like pattern of veins on both sides of a thick middle vein. She has not dug up the plant. Using the general relation in the chapter, what should she predict?
questions.a: A taproot, and seeds with two cotyledons. Reticulate venation generally goes with a taproot, and dicots, which have two cotyledons, have reticulate venation and taproots.
o: A taproot, and seeds with two cotyledons
A fibrous root, and seeds with two cotyledons
A taproot, and seeds with a single cotyledon
A fibrous root, and seeds with a single cotyledon

questions.q:
Rina in Ranchi recorded six plants from her school garden: P1, P2 and P3 have reticulate venation and taproots; P4 and P5 have parallel venation and fibrous roots; P6 has parallel venation and a taproot. She wrote 'relation between venation and roots is wrong' in her notebook, but her teacher asked her to be careful before changing a rule.
(a) How many plants follow the relation given in the chapter, and what percentage of the six is that?
(b) What number of cotyledons would you predict for P1 to P3 and for P4 and P5?
(c) Name two observations Rina could recheck about P6.
(d) Decide whether Rina should state that the relation is wrong or keep it as a general rule while she collects more plants. Give your reason.
questions.a: (a) 5 plants, 83.3%. (b) Two cotyledons for P1 to P3 (dicots) and one for P4 and P5 (monocots). (c) She could recheck the roots by digging carefully and the leaf venation by looking at the veins again. (d) Keep it as a general rule and test more plants: five of six agree and a single exception in a small sample does not overturn a general relation; but she should say it does not hold for every plant.
s: Followers: 3 + 2 = 5 of 6 = 83.3%
Dicot: two cotyledons; monocot: one cotyledon
Recheck the roots and the venation of P6
A judgement that weighs one exception against five agreeing plants

questions.q:
Two seed packets have lost their labels; one held chickpea and the other maize. After two days of soaking, seeds from packet X split into two parts when the coat is removed; seeds from packet Y show a single thin cotyledon.
(a) Which packet is maize, and why?
(b) The plants from packet X will be moved to the school garden. What kind of roots should the gardener expect to see while moving them, and why?
questions.a: (a) Packet Y: maize has a single thin cotyledon, so it is a monocot. (b) A taproot, one main root with small side roots: the packet X seeds have two cotyledons, and dicot plants have a taproot system.
s: Part (a): packet Y, one thin cotyledon as in maize
Part (b): taproot expected, because two cotyledons mean a dicot

questions.q:
For a science fair in Bhopal, five groups each soaked 4 chickpea seeds and 6 maize seeds and removed the coats of the chickpea seeds. The teacher says the display board can arrange the seedlings either by cotyledon number or by root type. Sorting by cotyledon number needs the seeds to be soaked for two or three days, while root type can be seen by carefully digging a seedling the same day.
(a) How many cotyledons did the five groups count in all?
(b) How many seedlings are expected to have taproots and how many fibrous roots?
(c) Why does a cotyledon grouping let the class predict other features too?
(d) Choose one arrangement for the display board and justify it, saying what you give up.
questions.a: (a) 70. (b) 20 taproot seedlings (chickpea) and 30 fibrous (maize). (c) Two cotyledons go with reticulate venation and a taproot, and one with parallel venation and fibrous roots, so one grouping predicts three features. (d) Cotyledon number gives more information but takes days; root type is quicker. Either choice is acceptable if the trade-off between predictive value and time is stated.
s: Cotyledons: 5 x (4 x 2 + 6 x 1) = 70
Taproot: 5 x 4 = 20; fibrous: 5 x 6 = 30
Cotyledon number is linked to venation and root type
A justified choice stating the trade-off between information and time

questions.q: Sarita sees that the leaves of a plant in the garden have parallel venation. She has not yet seen its roots. Which response is best justified by the chapter?
questions.a: Probably fibrous; she should dig to check, as the link is general. The chapter says generally parallel venation goes with fibrous roots; a general relation allows a prediction, not a guarantee.
o: Probably fibrous; she should dig to check, as the link is general
The roots must be a taproot, since parallel veins come from one main root
The roots must be fibrous in every plant, so digging up is not needed
Nothing can be said about the roots because leaves and roots are unrelated

questions.q: Zubin says: 'Maize has a single thin cotyledon, so its leaves must show reticulate venation.' Which reply corrects him best?
questions.a: Maize is a monocot, so its leaves are expected to show parallel venation. A single cotyledon makes maize a monocot, and monocots have parallel venation and fibrous roots; reticulate venation goes with dicots.
o: Maize is a monocot, so its leaves are expected to show parallel venation
He is right, because one cotyledon goes with a net of veins in leaves
Maize is a dicot, since its single cotyledon splits into two parts
Venation cannot be predicted from seeds, so he can say nothing at all

questions.q: The answer to a quiz question is: 'It is a monocot, so its leaves will have parallel veins.' Write a quiz question that leads to this answer. Your question must describe an observation of the seed or of the roots, not of the leaves, and must name a plant from the chapter that it could be about.
questions.a: For example: 'Lemongrass seedlings dug up from the nursery show a bunch of similar thin roots from the base of the stem. What group does the plant belong to, and what veins will its leaves have?' (A seed observation such as 'the soaked seed shows a single thin cotyledon', for maize or wheat, also works.)
s: Question describes a seed with one cotyledon or a fibrous root system
A matching plant from the chapter such as maize, wheat or lemongrass
The question asks for the group and the venation, so the given answer follows

questions.q:
Statement 1: Hibiscus leaves show reticulate venation.
