questions.a: Statement 1 only. Statement 2 is false because a monocot has a single cotyledon; statement 3 is false because lemongrass has parallel venation and fibrous roots.
o: Statement 1 only
Statement 2 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 2 and 3 only

questions.q:
The seed of a plant has two cotyledons. The plant is now growing in a pot that you must not disturb.
(a) Predict the venation and the root system of the plant.
(b) Which of your two predictions can you check today, and how?
questions.a: (a) Reticulate venation and a taproot (a dicot). (b) The venation: look at a leaf for a net-like pattern of veins on both sides of a thick middle vein. The roots cannot be seen without digging the plant out.
s: Part (a): reticulate venation and taproot for a dicot
Part (b): venation, by looking for net-like veins around a thick middle vein; roots need digging

questions.q:
Two seedlings in a school garden have lost their labels. Seedling S1 has one main root with small side roots. Seedling S2 has a bunch of similar-sized thin roots arising from the base of the stem.
(i) For S1, predict the venation of its leaves.
(ii) For S1, state the number of cotyledons and the group name.
(iii) For S2, predict the venation, the number of cotyledons and the group name.
(iv) Name one plant from the chapter that matches each seedling.
(v) The gardener must relabel both seedlings tomorrow after they are replanted, without digging them up again. Which part of each plant can she look at, and what should she see?
questions.a: (i) Reticulate. (ii) Two cotyledons, a dicot. (iii) Parallel venation, one cotyledon, a monocot. (iv) S1: chickpea, sadabahar, hibiscus or mustard; S2: wheat, lemongrass or grass. (v) The leaves: S1 should show a net-like pattern of veins around a thick middle vein; S2 should show veins running parallel.
s: S1 has a taproot, so reticulate venation is predicted
S1: dicot with two cotyledons
S2: parallel venation, one cotyledon and monocot
Examples from the chapter for each seedling
Leaves checked instead of roots: net-like veins for S1, parallel veins for S2

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The chickpea plant is classed as a dicotyledon.
Reason (R): Its seed splits into two parts and each part is called a cotyledon.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Both are true, and the seed having two cotyledons is exactly what makes a plant a dicot.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: Four seeds are soaked and opened. Seed P splits into two cotyledons, seed Q has a single thin cotyledon, seed R splits into two cotyledons and seed S has a single thin cotyledon. Which plants are expected to grow fibrous roots?
questions.a: Q and S only. A single cotyledon makes a plant a monocot, and monocots have a fibrous root system; P and R are dicots, with taproots.
o: Q and S only
P and R only
P, Q, R and S
Q only

questions.q: Pigeon and housefly fall in the same group when animals are grouped by movement and the body parts used. Which statement about them is most reasonable?
questions.a: Alike in how they move, but they may differ in size, shape and colour. The chapter says animals also differ in shape, size, structure, colour and other features, which can be used to group them in other ways.
o: Alike in how they move, but they may differ in size, shape and colour
They must be alike in every feature because they are in one group
They cannot be grouped on any other basis because their movement is the same
They are different animals only if one of them walks and the other cannot

questions.q:
Sunita copied the chapter's movement table into her notebook as: pigeon - flies - wings; goat - walks and jumps - legs and wings; fish - swims - legs; housefly - walks and flies - legs and wings. Her teacher marks each entry as fully correct or not.
(a) Which of the four entries are fully correct?
(b) Correct the incorrect entries.
(c) What percentage of the four entries were fully correct?
(d) Sunita argues that her pigeon entry is 'not wrong, only incomplete', so it should be counted as correct. Should the teacher count it? Give a reason, and say what her percentage would become if it were counted.
questions.a: (a) Only the housefly entry. (b) Pigeon: walks and flies, using legs and wings; goat: walks and jumps, using legs only; fish: swims, using fins. (c) 1 of 4 = 25%. (d) No: the entry leaves out walking and legs, so a reader would think the pigeon moves with wings alone, which the table contradicts; a record that leaves out a body part used for movement is not fully correct. Counted, it would be 2 of 4 = 50%.
s: Only the housefly entry is fully correct
Corrected entries for pigeon, goat and fish
One correct of four is 25%
Judgement: the incomplete entry misleads about legs and walking, so not counted (it would give 50%)

questions.q: Which animal and movement pair is NOT supported by the chapter's table of movements?
questions.a: A pigeon walks and flies using wings only. The table gives the pigeon legs and wings: walking needs the legs, so 'wings only' is not supported; the other three pairs match the table.
o: A pigeon walks and flies using wings only
A goat walks and jumps using legs
A housefly walks and flies using legs and wings
A fish swims using fins

questions.q: Mohit says: 'The pigeon and the housefly fly, so they use only their wings for movement.' Check his claim.
questions.a: No. The table shows that both walk and fly, and use legs and wings.
s: Verdict: wrong
Both also walk, so legs are used
Correct body parts: legs and wings

questions.q:
A school in Kozhikode is building an 'animal movement park' with one zone for each set of body parts used for movement. It has eight animal figures: goat, ant, cow (walks on four legs), pigeon, housefly, crow (flies and walks), and two kinds of fish. A zone board costs Rs 450 and each figure costs Rs 30. The budget is Rs 1,400.
(a) Name the zones needed and place the eight figures in them, using the body parts each animal uses.
(b) Find the cost of each zone and the amount by which the full park exceeds the budget.
(c) Plan A: drop the fins zone. Plan B: replace the three boards with one large board for Rs 1,000 that shows all three zones but has room for only 6 figures. Find the cost of each plan and check it against the budget.
(d) Choose plan A or plan B and justify it, saying what the park then fails to show.
questions.a: (a) Legs only: goat, ant, cow. Legs and wings: pigeon, housefly, crow. Fins: the two fish. (b) Legs only 450 + 3 x 30 = Rs 540; legs and wings Rs 540; fins 450 + 2 x 30 = Rs 510; total Rs 1,590, which is Rs 190 over. (c) Plan A: 540 + 540 = Rs 1,080; plan B: 1,000 + 6 x 30 = Rs 1,180; both fit within Rs 1,400. (d) Either is acceptable when justified. Plan A keeps all six land animals but shows no animal that moves with fins in water. Plan B shows all three sets of body parts, but two figures must go (for example one fish and one legs-only animal), so each zone has fewer examples.
s: Zones and placement: legs only (goat, ant, cow), legs and wings (pigeon, housefly, crow), fins (two fish)
Zone costs 540, 540, 510; total 1,590, Rs 190 over budget
Plan A Rs 1,080 and plan B Rs 1,180, both within budget
A justified choice that names what the park loses under it

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A fish and a goat use the same body part for movement.
Reason (R): The fish has fins for moving in water and the goat has legs for moving on grassy land.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true. A is false: the fish uses fins and the goat uses legs. R is true and shows why the body parts differ.
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

questions.q: Show that the five animals of the chapter's movement table (ant: legs; goat: legs; pigeon: legs and wings; housefly: legs and wings; fish: fins) cannot be put into only two groups so that each group has animals using exactly the same body parts.
questions.a: There are three different sets of body parts: legs only, legs and wings, and fins. Two groups cannot hold three different sets without mixing sets.
s: Identify the three distinct sets of body parts
Each group may hold only one set
Three sets need three groups

questions.q:
Fish have streamlined bodies and fins and live in water; goats have legs and live in grassy areas. A frog lives on land as well as in water. It has strong legs, and the toes of its back feet are joined by skin like a paddle.
(a) Which of the frog's features suits movement on land, and which suits movement in water?
(b) Using the fish and goat examples, explain why an animal that lives in both places has body parts that work in both.
questions.a: (a) The strong legs suit moving on land, as the goat's legs do; the paddle-like back feet push against water, as the fish's fins do. (b) An animal's body parts for movement suit its surroundings; a frog moves in water and on land, so it needs parts that work in each.
s: Part (a): legs for land, paddle-like feet for water
Part (b): body parts suit the surroundings, and the frog lives in both

questions.q:
Riya records the movement of 12 animals: 3 use fins, 5 use legs only and 4 use legs and wings.
(i) How many of her animals use legs in some way?
(ii) Riya writes: 'My list shows that every animal that moves uses legs.' Test her statement.
(iii) She wants each wall group to hold animals that use exactly the same body parts. How many groups does she need, and why?
(iv) Her teacher adds a crow (flies and walks). Which group does it join, and what fraction of the 13 animals is that group now?
(v) Riya concludes that legs are the most important body part for movement because most of her animals use them. Judge her conclusion.
questions.a: (i) 5 + 4 = 9. (ii) False: the 3 animals that use fins use no legs. (iii) Three: legs only, legs and wings, and fins are three different sets of body parts. (iv) The legs-and-wings group, which now holds 5 of 13 animals (5/13). (v) Not justified: her count only shows which body part is common in her list. Body parts for movement suit the surroundings, so for a fish in water fins are what work, and legs would not help it.
s: Legs used: 5 + 4 = 9
Statement false because the fins group uses no legs
Three distinct sets of body parts need three groups
Crow joins legs and wings: 5 of 13
Conclusion rejected: body parts suit surroundings, so a common part is not the most important for every animal

questions.q:
A teacher wants a wall chart for four animals: goat (walks and jumps, legs), pigeon (walks and flies, legs and wings), housefly (walks and flies, legs and wings) and fish (swims, fins).
(i) List the groups if the chart is made by type of movement.
(ii) How many animals appear in more than one such group?
(iii) List the groups if the chart is made by body parts used.
(iv) Does any animal appear in more than one of these groups?
(v) Which chart would you choose for a young class, and what do you lose by that choice?
questions.a: (i) Walk: goat, pigeon, housefly; fly: pigeon, housefly; jump: goat; swim: fish. (ii) Three: goat, pigeon and housefly. (iii) Legs: goat; legs and wings: pigeon, housefly; fins: fish. (iv) No. (v) Either choice is acceptable if justified: the body-part chart has no repeats; the movement chart shows more about how animals move.
s: Groups by movement type listed correctly
Goat, pigeon and housefly appear twice or more: three animals
Groups by body parts listed correctly
No animal repeats in the body-part chart
A justified choice stating what is lost

questions.q:
A student sorts goat, pigeon, housefly and fish into movement groups named 'jumps' and 'flies'.
(a) Place the goat, the pigeon and the housefly.
(b) The fish fits neither group. Name a group for it, with the body part it uses.
questions.a: (a) Jumps: goat; flies: pigeon and housefly. (b) A 'swims' group: the fish swims in water using its fins.
s: Part (a): goat in jumps; pigeon and housefly in flies
Part (b): swims, using fins

questions.q: True or False? If animals are grouped only by the body part used for movement, a goat and an ant fall in one group although they differ in size and shape. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. Both are listed as using legs for movement, and the chapter says animals differ in size, shape and other features.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: both use legs, and size and shape are different features

questions.q:
Statement 1: Every animal in the chapter's movement table uses legs, though some also use wings.
Statement 2: Pigeon and housefly can be put in the same group, since both walk and fly using legs and wings.
Statement 3: The pigeon and the housefly use their wings for walking as well as for flying.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 2 only. Statement 1 is false because the fish uses fins and no legs; statement 3 is false because walking uses the legs, while the wings are used for flying.
o: Statement 2 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
All three statements

questions.q: A class movement table writes 'legs' for the ant but leaves its type of movement blank. Pooja wants to put the ant in a 'walks and jumps' group with the goat. What should she do first?
questions.a: Watch an ant moving and record how it moves. The table gives only the body part; animals that use legs can walk, run, crawl, hop or jump, so the type of movement must be observed, not assumed from the goat's row.
o: Watch an ant moving and record how it moves
Put it with the goat, since all legged animals walk and jump
Put it with the fish, since both are small animals
Leave it out of every group, since it does not move

questions.q: A grasshopper walks and hops using its legs and flies using its wings. In a chart that groups the chapter's animals by the set of body parts used, it joins the pigeon and the ___.
questions.a: housefly

questions.q: Sohan says: 'Using the chapter's movement table, the pigeon and the housefly belong in a walks group together with the goat, even though they can fly.' Check his claim.
questions.a: Yes. The table records the goat as walking and jumping, and the pigeon and housefly as walking and flying, all using legs for walking. So all three fit a walks group; the pigeon and housefly can also be placed in a flies group.
s: Verdict: right
Evidence: goat walks and jumps; pigeon and housefly walk and fly
An animal with two types of movement can sit in two movement groups

questions.q: Maya writes in her movement table: 'Crow: flies and walks, using wings only.' Her friend asks her to correct it. Which correction fits the chapter's table of pigeon, goat and housefly?
questions.a: Add legs: walking uses legs, as for the pigeon. In the table, animals that walk (goat, pigeon, housefly) use legs, and the pigeon uses legs and wings for walking and flying.
o: Add legs: walking uses legs, as for the pigeon
Remove wings: any animal that walks has no wings
Replace wings by fins because birds also swim
Leave it as it is because one body part is enough for two movements

questions.q:
Chart P groups animals as: goat, ant | pigeon, housefly | fish. Chart Q groups them as: goat | pigeon, housefly | fish, and leaves out the ant.
(a) Name the basis used for each chart.
(b) Why could the ant be placed in chart P but not in chart Q, using the class movement table (ant: legs, type of movement not recorded)?
questions.a: (a) Chart P: the body parts used for movement (legs; legs and wings; fins). Chart Q: the type of movement (walks and jumps; walks and flies; swims). (b) Chart P needs only the body part, which is recorded for the ant; chart Q needs the type of movement, which the table leaves blank for the ant.
s: Part (a): P by body part used, Q by type of movement
Part (b): the ant's body part is known but its type of movement is not recorded

questions.q: Add one row to a table like the chapter's movement table for an animal you have seen yourself: give its name, how it moves, and the body part used. Say how it would be grouped.
questions.a: For example: crow, flies and walks, using legs and wings; grouped with pigeon.
s: An animal named with how it moves
A body part consistent with that movement
A grouping by movement or body part

questions.q:
A sparrow in the school yard hops along the ground on its legs and then flies off using its wings.
(a) Write its row for a movement table: type of movement and body parts used.
(b) In a chart grouped by the set of body parts used, would it sit with the goat? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Hops and flies; legs and wings. (b) No: it uses legs and wings, while the goat uses legs only; it would sit with the pigeon and the housefly.
s: Part (a): hops and flies, using legs and wings
Part (b): not with the goat, since its set of body parts is legs and wings

questions.q:
Match each animal of the chapter's movement table (column I) with the description that fits its row (column II).
1. Ant    a. Two body parts used for two types of movement, walking and flying
2. Goat    b. A body part is recorded, but no type of movement is written
3. Pigeon    c. Moves using fins, with no legs
4. Fish    d. One body part used for two types of movement, walking and jumping
questions.a: 1-b, 2-d, 3-a, 4-c. The table gives the ant legs with no movement written, the goat walking and jumping with legs, the pigeon walking and flying with legs and wings, and the fish fins.

questions.q:
Sea turtles live in the sea, camels in the hot or cold desert, and rhododendrons on mountains.
(a) Classify each habitat as terrestrial or aquatic.
(b) Which one of these three habitats could also be a habitat for a fish, and which need of the fish would the other two fail to provide?
questions.a: (a) Sea: aquatic; desert: terrestrial; mountains: terrestrial. (b) The sea: a fish lives in water and moves with fins, and the desert and the mountains are land habitats that cannot give it water to live and move in.
s: Part (a): sea aquatic; desert and mountains terrestrial
Part (b): the sea, because the land habitats lack the water a fish needs

questions.a: (i) Terrestrial: hot desert, snowy Himalayas, Nilgiris mountaintops; aquatic: ocean. (ii) Camel: the long legs and wide hooves let it walk on sand without sinking; fish: the streamlined body helps it swim in water. (iii) Moving: the camel's legs and hooves and the fish's streamlined body. Weather: the deodar's shape (snow) and the rhododendron's short height and small leaves (heavy wind). (iv) The hot desert is very cold at night after a hot day; the mountains get frequent snowfall. Only the deodar's conical shape with sloping branches deals with the cold, by letting snow slide off; the camel's hooves are for sand. (v) Conditions differ from region to region, and plants and animals have adaptations that fit their own region's conditions, so different kinds live in the ocean and in the desert.
s: Ocean aquatic; desert and both mountain habitats terrestrial
Camel's legs and hooves for sand; fish's streamlined body for swimming
Movement features (camel, fish) against weather features (deodar, rhododendron)
Cold nights in the hot desert against snowfall on mountains; only the deodar's shape deals with cold
Biodiversity varies because conditions differ and each living thing is adapted to its region

questions.q:
Match each living thing and its feature (column I) with the condition of its region that the feature helps it survive (column II).
1. Cactus: thick, fleshy stems    a. Frequent snowfall
2. Deodar: conical shape, sloping branches    b. Heat with very little water
3. Hot-desert camel: long legs, wide hooves    c. Heavy winds on mountain tops
4. Nilgiris rhododendron: short, small leaves    d. Soft sand underfoot
questions.a: 1-b, 2-a, 3-d, 4-c. Fleshy stems store water in the hot desert, the deodar's shape lets snow slide off, long legs and wide hooves keep the camel from sinking in sand, and short height with small leaves helps rhododendrons through heavy winds.

questions.q:
A botanical garden in the Nilgiris compared 10 rhododendron plants from the Shola forests on a windy mountaintop with 10 from the mountains near Sikkim. Average height: Nilgiris 1.2 m and Sikkim 3.1 m. Average length of a leaf: Nilgiris 6 cm and Sikkim 11 cm. The garden wants to plant rhododendrons on an exposed, windy ridge. A tourist officer asks for the taller Sikkim type, which flowers within two years and draws visitors; the Nilgiris type grows slowly and is expected to give only a few flowers in its first four years.
(a) By how many metres is the Nilgiris plant shorter, and what percentage of the Sikkim height is that (one decimal place)?
(b) By what percentage are the Nilgiris leaves shorter than the Sikkim leaves (one decimal place)?
(c) What do the shorter height and smaller leaves help the Nilgiris plants to do?
(d) Decide which type to plant on the ridge, or whether to mix them, and justify your choice.
questions.a: (a) 1.9 m, 61.3%. (b) 45.5%. (c) Survive the heavy winds on mountain tops. (d) Either plan is acceptable when justified. The Nilgiris type has the height and leaves that let it survive heavy winds, but few flowers for four years; the Sikkim type gives early flowers and visitors but risks damage on an exposed ridge. A mix, with Sikkim plants in the most sheltered spots, is also defensible if the risk is named.
s: Difference: 3.1 - 1.2 = 1.9 m, which is 61.3% of 3.1
Leaf difference: (11 - 6)/11 x 100 = 45.5%
Survival through heavy winds on mountaintops
A justified plan that weighs survival in wind against early flowers and visitors

questions.q: A record card reads: 'Habitat: aquatic. Moves with fins. Streamlined body.' Write a short description (two or three sentences) of where and how this animal lives, as Sagar might have described it after his trip to the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Name the habitat group and give one more aquatic habitat it could belong to.
questions.a: For example: 'Near the Andaman and Nicobar Islands I watched colourful fish swimming in the ocean. Their streamlined bodies and fins help them move through the water.' The habitat is aquatic; other aquatic habitats are ponds, lakes and rivers.
s: A description set in water that uses the fins and streamlined body for swimming
Habitat group named as aquatic
One more aquatic habitat such as a pond, lake or river

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Camels of the hot desert can survive many days without drinking water.
Reason (R): Camels of the hot desert have long legs and wide hooves.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. Both are true, but long legs and wide hooves help the camel walk without sinking in sand; they do not explain surviving without water.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: True or False? The habitat of a plant or animal is only the food it eats. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. A habitat is the place where a plant or animal lives, and it provides food, water, air, shelter and other needs.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: a habitat is the place where it lives, providing food, water, air and shelter

questions.q:
A village pond in Karnataka is surrounded by grass. A class counted 18 kinds of animals around it: 9 kinds live only in the pond, 6 live only on the bank, and the others live in the pond as well as on the bank. The panchayat plans to fill half the pond for a bus stand, which will leave less water for the pond kinds.
(a) How many kinds are amphibians?
(b) What percentage of the 18 kinds depend on the pond water, either wholly or partly (one decimal place)?
(c) The pond provides food, water, air and shelter. Which of these is most at risk for the pond-only kinds if half the pond is filled, and why?
(d) Suggest a decision for the panchayat, and justify it using your answers.
questions.a: (a) 3. (b) 12/18 = 66.7%. (c) Water (and with it shelter): the pond-only kinds live in the water, so less water leaves them less room to live, shelter and find food. (d) Either shift the bus stand away from the pond or fill only a small part of it; two thirds of the kinds use the pond, so filling half of it harms most of them, though the bus stand serves a real need.
s: Amphibians: 18 - 9 - 6 = 3
Pond-dependent kinds: 9 + 3 = 12, which is 66.7%
Water (and shelter in it) named as most at risk for kinds that live only in the pond
A decision that weighs the bus stand against the loss of habitat

questions.q: Rita says: 'Camels in both the hot desert and the cold desert have humps that store food, so they have the same number of humps.' Check her claim.
questions.a: Partly right. Humps store food in both, but the hot-desert camel has one hump and the cold-desert camel of Ladakh has two humps.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: humps store food in both kinds
Wrong part: one hump in the hot desert, two in the cold desert

questions.q:
Statement 1: The fleshy stems of desert plants can store water and help them tolerate hot conditions.
Statement 2: The conical shape and sloping branches of deodar trees help snow slide off easily.
Statement 3: A camel of the cold desert of Ladakh has long legs and wide hooves to avoid sinking in sand.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 2 only. Statement 3 is false: long legs and wide hooves belong to the camel of the hot desert; the Ladakh camel has shorter legs.
o: Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 3 only
All three statements

questions.q: Rhododendrons in the Shola forests of the Nilgiris are shorter with smaller leaves, while those Pema saw in the mountains near Sikkim were taller. Which conclusion does this example support?
questions.a: The same plant kind can show different features in different regions. The chapter says even plants such as rhododendrons may show different features in different regions to survive the conditions of those regions.
o: The same plant kind can show different features in different regions
Rhododendrons can grow only in the Nilgiris and not near Sikkim
Taller plants are always better adapted to mountains than shorter ones
Smaller leaves help plants store water in a hot desert

questions.q:
In a hot desert near Jaisalmer, the sand is scorching in the afternoon and the same place is very cold at night.
(a) What must the plants and animals of such a place be able to do?
(b) A gardener says: 'Any plant that likes warm weather will grow here if I water it every day.' Give one reason, from the chapter, why such a plant may still fail.
(c) Name the feature of desert plants that the chapter says helps them tolerate the hot conditions.
questions.a: (a) Tolerate and survive both the hot conditions of the day and the cold conditions of the night. (b) Watering helps with heat and dryness but not with the very cold nights; a plant without features to tolerate the cold may not survive. (c) Fleshy stems that store water.
s: Part (a): tolerate both hot days and cold nights
Part (b): watering does not protect against the cold nights
Part (c): fleshy stems that store water

questions.q: A veterinary student in Rajasthan wants to know which feature of the camels there helps them save water, so that they can live many days without drinking. Which feature should she point to?
questions.a: Little urine, dry dung and almost no sweat. Kashi's observation is that small urine, dry dung and no sweating mean little water is lost; legs and hooves help on sand and the hump stores food.
o: Little urine, dry dung and almost no sweat
The long legs that lift the body above the sand
The wide hooves that spread the weight on sand
The single hump that stores food

questions.q: A village fills in a small pond to widen the road. Which statement best describes what the fish and plants of the pond lose?
questions.a: Their habitat, giving food, water, air and shelter. A habitat is the place where plants and animals live, providing food, water, air and shelter; adaptation is a survival feature.
o: Their habitat, giving food, water, air and shelter
Their adaptation, which is the place where they live
Their biodiversity, which is the place where they live
Their terrestrial habitat, the land on which they lived

questions.q: A survey team lists the kinds of animals around a lake: 14 kinds are seen only in the water, 9 kinds only on land, and the list holds 27 kinds in all. The number of amphibian kinds on the list is ___.
A student sorts seven habitat cards: desert, pond, mountain, river, grassland, ocean, and 'pond with its muddy bank, home of frogs'. Which sorting follows the chapter?
questions.a: Land: desert, mountain, grassland; water: pond, river, ocean; last card in both. Deserts, mountains and grasslands are terrestrial and ponds, rivers and oceans aquatic; frogs live in water as well as on land, so that card belongs to both.
o: Land: desert, mountain, grassland; water: pond, river, ocean; last card in both
Land: desert, mountain, grassland, last card; water: pond, river, ocean
Land: desert, mountain; water: pond, river, ocean, grassland, last card
Land: desert, grassland, river; water: pond, mountain, ocean; last card in water

questions.q:
Sagar saw huge whales and colourful fish in the ocean near the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
(a) Name the habitat group of the ocean.
(b) A classmate says: 'The whales and the fish share one habitat, so they must have the same size and shape.' Is he right? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Aquatic. (b) No. Many types of plants and animals may share the same habitat, and animals differ from one another in size and shape; sharing a habitat does not make them alike.
s: Part (a): aquatic
Part (b): No, many kinds share one habitat and still differ in size and shape

questions.q: Leena says: 'Mountains are all terrestrial habitats, so every plant that lives on a mountain will have the same adaptation.' Check her claim using two plants from the chapter.
questions.a: No. Deodar trees on snowy mountains have a conical shape and sloping branches that let snow slide off, while rhododendrons on windy Nilgiris mountaintops are short with small leaves to survive heavy winds. The conditions differ (snowfall against wind), so the adaptations differ.
s: Verdict: wrong
Deodar: conical shape and sloping branches for snowfall
Rhododendron: short with small leaves for heavy wind, so different conditions give different adaptations

questions.q: True or False? The conical shape and sloping branches of a deodar tree are its habitat. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. The shape and branches are an adaptation, a special feature that helps the deodar survive snowfall; its habitat is the place where it lives, the mountains.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the shape is an adaptation; the habitat is the mountains where it lives

questions.q:
A tour company plans camel treks in Ladakh. It offers a camel with these features: one hump, long legs with wide hooves, and short hair on the head and neck.
(i) Which feature of this camel matches a camel of Ladakh? (Check each of the three.)
(ii) For the hump: what does a Ladakh camel have instead, and what happens to it in late winter?
(iii) For the legs: why are the Ladakh camel's shorter legs better on its terrain?
(iv) For the hair: what does the Ladakh camel grow, and how does it help?
(v) Should the company use this camel for winter treks in Ladakh? Give a judgement that uses the idea of adaptation.
questions.a: (i) None of the three: the camel described has the features of a hot-desert camel. (ii) Two humps that store food; they shrink in late winter as the stored food is used when little food is available. (iii) Shorter legs let a camel walk easily in mountainous regions; long legs and wide hooves suit sandy deserts. (iv) Long hair from head to neck, which helps it survive the cold winters. (v) No: adaptations are the special features that let an animal survive in a particular region, and this camel's features fit the hot desert, not the mountains and cold winters of Ladakh.
s: None of the three features matches a Ladakh camel
Two humps that shrink in late winter as stored food is used
Shorter legs suit walking in mountains, long legs and wide hooves suit sand
Long hair from head to neck for cold winters
Judgement: not suited, because adaptations fit the region the animal lives in

questions.q:
A class groups five animals by habitat: sea turtle, camel, goat, fish and frog.
(a) Place each animal as living in a terrestrial habitat, an aquatic habitat, or both.
(b) The frog and the goat both move with legs. Why do they still go into different habitat groups?
questions.a: (a) Aquatic: sea turtle, fish; terrestrial: camel, goat; both: frog (an amphibian). (b) Grouping by habitat uses where an animal lives, not how it moves: the goat lives on grassy land, while the frog lives in water as well as on land.
s: Part (a): sea turtle and fish aquatic, camel and goat terrestrial, frog both
Part (b): habitat grouping is by where it lives, not by body parts for movement

questions.q:
Match each conservation effort (column I) with what it does (column II).
1. Project Tiger (1973)    a. Restore the population of the Cheetah
2. Cheetah Reintroduction Project (2022)    b. Safeguard the habitats of the Great Indian Bustard
3. Protected Areas in Gujarat, Rajasthan and Maharashtra    c. Keep forest patches undisturbed through the local community
4. Sacred groves    d. Protect the declining population of the Bengal Tiger
questions.a: 1-d, 2-a, 3-b, 4-c. Project Tiger protects the Bengal Tiger, the Cheetah project restores the Cheetah, the Protected Areas safeguard the Bustard's habitats, and sacred groves are forest patches protected by local communities.

questions.q: In a village of the Western Ghats, a woodcutter is stopped by the elders from cutting a tree in a patch of forest that has never been disturbed. What best describes this patch?
questions.a: A sacred grove kept undisturbed by the community. Sacred groves are undisturbed patches of forest protected by the local community, where no one may harm animals or cut trees.
o: A sacred grove kept undisturbed by the community
A Protected Area declared for the Great Indian Bustard
A patch fenced by the government for Project Tiger
A garden of medicinal plants grown by one family

questions.q: In a village, a 10-hectare forest patch is called 'the old grove', but every winter the villagers cut some of its trees for firewood and graze goats inside it. Show that this patch cannot be a sacred grove as the chapter describes one.
questions.a: A sacred grove is an undisturbed patch of forest protected by the local community, where no one is allowed to harm animals, cut trees or disturb the area. In this patch trees are cut every winter and goats graze inside, so it is disturbed and the community is not protecting it; a name alone does not make it a sacred grove.
s: A sacred grove is undisturbed and protected by the community
No cutting of trees or disturbing of the area is allowed there
Yearly cutting and grazing disturb the patch, so it cannot be one

questions.q:
A herbal-medicine maker asks the elders of a village for permission to dig up roots of medicinal plants in their sacred grove.
(a) Would the elders be likely to allow it? Give the reason from the chapter.
(b) Explain why protecting the grove is in his own interest over the years.
questions.a: (a) No: in a sacred grove the community allows no one to harm animals, cut trees or disturb the area, and digging up plants disturbs it. (b) The grove is home to numerous medicinal plants; kept undisturbed, it continues to shelter them, while digging them out would reduce them.
s: Part (a): not allowed, since the grove must not be disturbed
Part (b): the grove keeps sheltering numerous medicinal plants only if undisturbed

questions.q: Write a short conversation (four or five lines) between a grandparent and a child in which they find out that a bird the grandparent saw often in childhood is now rarely seen. The conversation must give the chapter's reason for such a change and one thing the family or village could do about it.
questions.a: For example: Child: 'Nani, did you see sparrows when you were small?' Nani: 'Every day, near the big pond and the bushes behind our house.' Child: 'Why are there so few now?' Nani: 'The pond was filled and the bushes cleared for houses, so they lost their homes and food.' Child: 'Then let us keep the bushes in our lane and ask the panchayat not to fill the last pond.'
s: A believable exchange about a once-common plant or animal now rarely seen
The reason: its habitat was damaged, taking away homes and food
A sensible step that protects the habitat

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Cheetah Reintroduction Project was initiated in India in 2022.
Reason (R): The population of the Cheetah had declined in India due to loss of natural habitats caused by human activities.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. The chapter says the project was initiated in 2022 to restore the population of the Cheetah, which had declined because of habitat loss.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
A wildlife officer says: 'We will bring in more cheetahs every year, so the problem of their decline is solved.'
(a) Using the cause of decline given in the chapter, explain why this may not be enough.
(b) Which step taken for the Great Indian Bustard deals with that cause directly?
questions.a: (a) The Cheetah declined because its natural habitats were lost to human activities; animals brought into places without enough habitat would still lack homes, food and other resources. (b) Declaring its habitats in Gujarat, Rajasthan and Maharashtra as Protected Areas.
s: Part (a): the cause was habitat loss, which more animals do not fix
Part (b): the Bustard's habitats declared Protected Areas

questions.q: A grassland where many birds and insects lived is turned into a plot for buildings. Which sequence follows the chapter's reasoning about what happens next?
questions.a: Habitat damaged; homes, food and resources lost; biodiversity falls. Damage to habitats results in loss of homes, food and other resources, which leads to loss of biodiversity.
o: Habitat damaged; homes, food and resources lost; biodiversity falls
Biodiversity is lost first, and then the habitat is damaged by the loss
The animals gain new food and homes on the plot, and biodiversity rises
The habitat is unaffected, since only the human activities on it change

questions.q:
A district has 40 forest patches: 12 are sacred groves protected by their communities, 8 are Protected Areas, and the other 20 have no protection. In ten years, a quarter of the unprotected patches are damaged; no protected patch is damaged.
(i) How many patches are protected, and what percentage of the 40 is that?
(ii) How many patches are damaged, and what percentage of all 40 is that?
(iii) A councillor says: 'Only one patch in eight was damaged, so the district's biodiversity is safe.' Evaluate his claim using what damage does to a habitat.
(iv) Which kind of protection in this district depends on the people living nearby rather than on the government, and what do they do?
(v) Recommend what should be done with the unprotected patches that are still undamaged, giving one reason and one difficulty.
questions.a: (i) 12 + 8 = 20, which is 50%. (ii) 20 x 1/4 = 5 patches, which is 12.5% (one in eight). (iii) Not safe: in each damaged patch the plants and animals lost their homes, food and other resources, so biodiversity was lost there; and 15 more patches remain unprotected. (iv) The sacred groves: local communities keep them undisturbed and allow no one to harm animals or cut trees. (v) For example, protect the 15 undamaged patches, as community groves or Protected Areas, because the protected patches suffered no damage; a difficulty is that people who use these patches for wood or grazing may lose out.
s: Protected: 20 patches, 50%
Damaged: 5 patches, 12.5%
Claim rejected: damaged patches lost homes, food and resources, and 15 patches are still unprotected
Sacred groves, kept undisturbed by local communities
A recommendation for the 15 patches with a reason and a difficulty

questions.q: In one state, the number of Great Indian Bustards is falling while the grasslands where they live are being ploughed for new fields. Which measure deals with the cause that the chapter gives?
questions.a: Declare the grasslands where the bird lives a Protected Area. The decline is caused by loss of natural habitat; the chapter says the Bustard's habitats have been declared Protected Areas in Gujarat, Rajasthan and Maharashtra. Feeding a few birds does not save their habitat, and trees would change the grassland.
o: Declare the grasslands where the bird lives a Protected Area
Keep a few birds in a pen and feed them grain every day
Start a project to count the tigers in the state's forests
Plant tall trees across the grassland to give the birds shelter

questions.q: A 2022 newspaper headline says the Cheetah Reintroduction Project began 'exactly half a century after Project Tiger'. Using the years in the chapter, the two projects actually began ___ years apart.
Ravi's grandfather says he used to see a bird often as a child but now seldom sees it. Which explanation fits the chapter?
questions.a: Its habitat may have been damaged, so it lost home and food. The chapter says such changes often happen when habitats are damaged, which causes loss of homes, food and other resources.
o: Its habitat may have been damaged, so it lost home and food
Birds always disappear from a place when a person grows old
Biodiversity always increases whenever a habitat is damaged
The bird has moved into a sacred grove and will never leave

questions.q:
Project Tiger aims at the Bengal Tiger, while for the Great Indian Bustard the places where it lives in three states have been declared Protected Areas.
(a) Which of the two measures is described as protecting a population and which as protecting habitats?
(b) Why can protecting a habitat help more than one kind of plant or animal?
questions.a: (a) Project Tiger protects the declining population of one animal, the Bengal Tiger; the Protected Areas protect the Bustard's habitats. (b) Many types of plants and animals may share the same habitat, and the habitat provides their food, water, air and shelter; keeping it safe protects all of them.
s: Part (a): Project Tiger a population, the Bustard measure habitats
Part (b): many kinds share one habitat that meets their needs

questions.q: Meera says: 'The Great Indian Bustard is being helped even though no project named after it appears in the chapter, because the places where it lives have been protected.' Check her claim.
questions.a: Yes. The chapter names Project Tiger and the Cheetah Reintroduction Project, but for the Great Indian Bustard its habitats have been declared Protected Areas in Gujarat, Rajasthan and Maharashtra. Since its decline was caused by loss of natural habitat, protecting the habitat helps it.
s: Verdict: right
Its habitats were declared Protected Areas in three states
This targets the cause of its decline, habitat loss

questions.q:
A district's grasslands covered 9,600 hectares in 2005 and 6,000 hectares in 2025, as fields and roads spread. Bird surveys found 48 kinds of grassland birds in 2005 and 34 kinds in 2025. About 300 herder families graze their sheep on the grassland that is left. The state can declare all 6,000 hectares a Protected Area with no grazing, or protect 3,000 hectares strictly and allow grazing on the rest.
(a) Find the percentage of grassland lost and the percentage of bird kinds lost (one decimal place).
(b) Using the chapter, explain how the first loss can lead to the second.
(c) One of the birds whose numbers have fallen is a large bird whose habitats in Gujarat, Rajasthan and Maharashtra have been declared Protected Areas. Name it and say what the declaration protects.
(d) Choose one plan and justify it, saying who or what pays the cost of your choice.
questions.a: (a) Grassland: 3,600/9,600 = 37.5%; bird kinds: 14/48 = 29.2%. (b) When a habitat is damaged, its plants and animals lose their homes, food and other resources, which leads to loss of biodiversity, so fewer bird kinds remain. (c) The Great Indian Bustard; the declaration protects its habitat, the place where it lives. (d) Either plan is acceptable when justified. Full protection keeps the most habitat for the birds, but the 300 herder families lose their grazing. Half protection lets the families keep grazing, but the birds keep only 3,000 hectares strictly safe.
s: Losses: 37.5% of grassland and 29.2% of bird kinds
Habitat damage removes homes, food and resources, so biodiversity falls
Great Indian Bustard; the Protected Area safeguards its habitat
A justified plan that names who bears the cost (birds or herders)

questions.q:
A village has two plans. Plan A: plant 500 saplings of one fast-growing tree on a cleared plot. Plan B: leave a 3-hectare patch of old mixed forest undisturbed, as a sacred grove is kept.
(a) Which plan better protects biodiversity, and why?
(b) Give one benefit of plan A that the village might still want.

(c) Which rule of a sacred grove, as the chapter describes it, would the road through the middle break?
(d) Decide which road the village should choose, with a reason that uses the numbers, and say what is given up.
questions.a: (a) 25%. (b) 30% medicinal; 162 kinds in all. (c) In a sacred grove no one is allowed to cut trees, harm animals or disturb the area; clearing 1.5 hectares for a road cuts trees and disturbs the grove. (d) Take the road around if the village can raise the Rs 18 lakh, since the grove shelters 162 kinds and a quarter of it would be cleared; the cost is money and the longer walk. A justified choice that names what is given up

questions.q:
A hill village has an undisturbed 5-hectare forest patch full of medicinal plants and birds; no tigers live there. A district officer proposes to make it part of a government Protected Area; the village elders want to keep looking after it themselves as their sacred grove.
(i) Under each plan, who would protect the patch?
(ii) A villager suggests asking for the patch to be brought under Project Tiger instead. Explain why that scheme does not fit this patch.
(iii) What does the sacred-grove tradition already forbid, and how does that protect the medicinal plants?
(iv) What do the Great Indian Bustard's Protected Areas and a sacred grove have in common as ways of protecting biodiversity?
(v) Judge which plan the village should prefer, giving one reason and one risk of your choice.
questions.a: (i) Protected Area: the government; sacred grove: the local community. (ii) Project Tiger was started to protect the declining population of the Bengal Tiger, and no tigers live in this patch. (iii) No one may harm animals, cut trees or disturb the area, so the medicinal plants are left to grow undisturbed. (iv) Both protect the place where plants and animals live (the habitat), not a single animal alone. (v) For example: keep it as a sacred grove, since the community already keeps it undisturbed and can start at once; a risk is that the community alone may find it hard to stop an outside project. Choosing the Protected Area is also acceptable with a reason and a risk.
s: Government for the Protected Area, community for the sacred grove
Project Tiger is for the Bengal Tiger, which is absent here
Grove rules forbid harm, cutting and disturbance, which shelters the medicinal plants
Both protect the habitat rather than one animal
A judgement with one reason and one risk
